job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior controls engineer at a company in Newcastle that services wind turbines. I've been there four months on a graduate contract. I read fault logs from turbines, write small scripts to sort the alarms, and every second week I go out to a site with a senior engineer called Anders and climb up a tower. I did electrical engineering, passed with an average mark, and my final project was a battery charger that only half worked. I share a flat with two friends from uni. I use an AI assistant every day to write scripts and explain manuals. My dad's a bus mechanic and my mum works in a bank branch, and neither can lend me money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, that's roughly how I'd planned it. At work I'd tell Anders the scripts are a bit quicker with the helper, but the turbines still need people on them. To friends I'd say nobody's job changes much, so enjoy the quiet. Online I'd post nothing, I'm bad at posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change my money problem. I earn the lowest wage in the team, my loan repayment is big, and the firm depends on two big wind-farm contracts. If one is lost, they'd cut graduates first. I've seen it happen to the group before mine. So I'm tense, even though AI isn't the cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get on every site visit I can, because that's where the real learning is. I'd keep using the AI daily to be quick at the desk work. I'd freelance on weekends, writing small control scripts for local firms, which a friend has offered me. And I'd save £80 a month for a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine on the surface. Underneath I'm uneasy about the contracts. I'd say a bit anxious, though I don't show it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the group before you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three graduates were let go after a contract ended, with a week's notice. Two of them are still looking, one is stacking shelves at a supermarket. I met Kasia (a former colleague) for a coffee and she said she'd stopped telling people what her degree was in. That stuck with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the freelance work involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend runs a small brewery and wants its tanks to log temperature and send an alert. I'd write the script, test it on-site and charge about £400. It isn't much, but it's mine, and it could lead to more. I'd have to do it in weekends and be careful about my firm's rules on outside work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fair, and it's good for people who adapt. At work I'd say let's use the AI to read all the turbine alarm logs first, so engineers only see what matters. To friends I'd say learn the tools or someone who does will do your job. Online I'd say retraining money should go to people who can't just teach themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm in a good position compared to other graduates, because my job has a physical half. Desk work, like reading logs and writing scripts, gets quickly automated. The site work stays for years, since robots don't climb towers yet. But I'm still new, and a firm facing a squeeze might just not hire my replacement when I leave. So I think I'm okay, and I still worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be the person who builds the alarm-sorting tool, using AI. That makes me the one who understands it. I'd also ask to be certified for tower climbing and high-voltage work, which takes a few weeks and costs the firm, not me. I'd put some money into a cheap online course in machine learning. And I'd keep the freelance work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a good kind of pressure. I'm a bit excited. The worry is there, but it's smaller than the energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the firm pay for your tower certificates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they need climbers, and they already pay for the senior ones. Anders told me he'd put my name forward if I asked. I'd ask in the first month, with a plan: I want to be able to go out alone by next summer. That's a clear thing to say yes to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend in a pure desk job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say find a part of the work that's physical or involves dealing with people face to face. And use the AI so heavily that your boss can't imagine you without it. It's not an answer for everyone, but it's what I'd do if I were them. I'd also say save more than you think you need.

I'd say retraining money should go to people who **can't** teach themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is wild, and that we should treat it like an emergency. At work I'd ask Anders directly how the firm plans to survive it. To friends I'd say get money, get skills with your hands, and get close to your family. Online I'd back a public safety net and a pause on firms laying off graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my desk half disappears quickly, and my site half is what's left. I'd have maybe three years more of that, until robots can climb a tower, around 2031. But a firm with an AGI could simply buy the monitoring and send fewer people. I'm afraid the number of site jobs shrinks even if they don't vanish. And I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every penny and take on extra freelance work, to build a cushion in the first six months. I'd ask to go full-time on site work, and I'd get every certificate. I'd move into a cheaper flat, maybe back with my parents for a few months. And I'd look at jobs in the power grid, solar and batteries, where people still need to be on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a very loud alarm that nobody can turn off. I'm focused, though, not frozen. I'd say my head is full of lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might move back with your parents. How would they react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would clear out the box room within an hour. My mum would worry about me, which I'd find harder. They live in a small house in Gateshead and it would be tight, but it's possible. I'd keep paying them something, even £150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your lists comes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. A cushion of three months, then the certificates, then the job applications in the grid and solar. I put money first because without it I can't take a risk. If I had £3,000 I'd feel brave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, and anyone who uses it well can come out fine. At work I'd say let's plan which jobs the firm needs in 2031 and train people for those. To friends I'd say learn to run the machines, not just the screens. Online I'd say that firms and governments should share the cost of retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not scared. I'm uneasy, but I think I'm on a good path: I understand the AI tools, I can climb a tower, and I'm building freelance work. If I keep doing that, I'd be a hard person to replace. The thing I can't control is whether the firm survives that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to become a full site engineer within two years. I'd grow the freelance work into a proper small business, with one or two regular clients. I'd save £150 a month for a deposit and a cushion. And I'd keep learning how to build AI tools for control systems, because I think that's where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like I've got a decent map. I'm a bit proud of that. I know it can change, but for now I feel okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up the idea of a small business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the freelance work cost me my main job, or if I couldn't get more than a couple of clients. I'd treat it as an experiment with a time limit, say eighteen months. If it isn't earning £500 a month by then, I'd focus on the main career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're proud of the map. What would you tell someone who's lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start with one small thing that you can show. A script, a certificate, a job on a site. And don't wait for a perfect plan. I made mine from what was in front of me, and I changed it three times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and that it's exciting. At work I'd say let's think about what turbines need in 2036. To friends I'd say stay curious and keep one foot in the real world. Online I'd say policies for retraining and for who owns the AI should be argued about now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd say I'm calm. Ten years is long enough to be a good engineer, pay off my loan and have savings. I could even run my own small firm, doing control systems for wind and solar. I do wonder who'll own the AI, because if it's a few companies, the benefits won't spread. That's a worry, but it isn't mine alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work up to a senior engineer role, then think about going independent. I'd save for a deposit on a flat. I'd take a part-time master's in control systems if the firm helps. And I'd probably do some volunteering on a community energy scheme, because I like the idea of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bright. I'm aware that I'm lucky to be able to say that. I'd still have my moments at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the three-in-the-morning moments about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. The loan balance, the rent, and whether Anders's firm keeps me on. I wake up and do sums in my head. They pass by the time I've made tea, but they're real, and I'd rather say it than pretend I'm unbothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a community energy scheme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like that it's local, and that people own part of it. If AI makes energy cheaper, I want the benefits to go to more than shareholders. It's a small way of voting with my time. I'd also meet people who could hire me one day, which I'm not shy about.

I'd tell friends to keep one foot in the **real world**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My strengths, the tools and the tower, take time to build, and two years is too short to do it with no savings. What would help is a safety net that works in weeks, paid certificates, and firms that don't dump their graduates when a contract ends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think engineers are all fine. We're not, we're just quiet about it. A lot of graduates I know are doing a job they didn't plan for, owing money they can't see how to repay. If someone asked them honestly, they'd say they're scared.

headlineQuote: A lot of graduates I know are doing a job they didn't plan for, owing money they can't see how to repay.
portrait: Rosa is a 22-year-old electrical engineering graduate working as a **junior controls engineer** servicing wind turbines in Newcastle.
She is centrist and adaptive: she uses AI daily, takes risks, and freelances writing control scripts.
Her cushion is thin, with a big loan and parents who cannot lend money, so contract **worries** shadow everything.
Half her job is physical tower work, which she uses as protection.
Two years alarms her, while ten years makes her calm enough to dream of her own firm.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because her strengths take time to build and she has no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A safety net that works in **weeks**, paid certificates, and firms that keep graduates when contracts end.
